title: Been building a cryto bot for a few months, simulated money not live yet, still testing before I drop real money into this.
author: IllustratorSouth4671
selftext:
Quick version of where I've been:

**V1**: looked amazing on paper (\~99% win rate), turned out that was mostly an illusion — a lot of "wins" were really just me adding margin to rescue losing positions instead of letting them actually close, so it wasn't a real edge.

**V2**: fixed that, added real risk controls — capped leverage, capped how many positions could stack on one coin, capped total exposure across everything. Then a correlated crash hit 3-4 coins at once on the same day and wiped out most of the gains anyway, because nothing was actually cutting losses early.

BY RESCUE I MEAN ADDING MORE MARGIN TO A LOSING POSTIOK TO AVOID LIQUIDATION INSTEAD OF LETTING IT CLOSE ON A LOSS

**V3 (current)**: testing a grid of \~28 variants at once — different capital-compounding rates, different reactions to margin calls (match it / only rescue if I'm also deep underwater / never rescue and just exit), and a separate batch testing hard stop-losses at -15%/-25%/-35% with leverage capped at 10x, 40x, and uncapped.

Here's the part that's actually confusing me: my real win rate is genuinely decent, some days like 3 days ago I achieved a 120/119 and normally I get something like 60%-86%. 

But I'm still net negative overall, because my average loser is roughly 4x the size of my average winner. Winners tend to close out modestly, losers tend to run deep before I do anything about it.

I added hard stop losses to fix that, and the data so far actually supports it. Tighter stops are losing less than looser ones, and lower leverage is losing less than higher leverage.

But the stop loss versions are still net negative overall, just less negative. It feels like I'm treating the symptom (cutting losses at a fixed %) without fixing the actual cause (letting the position get that bad in the first place, or being wrong about entries in a way that a stop can't fully rescue).

So for anyone who's dealt with this: is a fixed % stop-loss just fundamentally the wrong tool here? Should I be trying to predict which trades are likely to go bad early instead of reacting after the fact? Trailing stops, volatility-based stops, position sizing changes, something else entirely? Genuinely stuck on what the next lever to pull is. 

Any ideas welcome.

comments.author: fomoz
comments.body:
I don't know how your bot works but you'll probably be better off with a 1-2% SL by default. I'm not sure why you think 15%+ SL is a good idea. 

Also, you win rate doesn't matter. You can lose money with a high WR and make money with a low WR.

replies.author: IllustratorSouth4671
replies.body: Beacause it varies sometimes 25% -40% of my trades dip before they make profit. So by cutting them off early I’m cutting off potential winners

replies.author: fomoz
replies.body:
For fuck's sakes, it shouldn't dip 25%. Think about it.

It means you have no edge, you're just trying to over fit.

replies.author: IllustratorSouth4671
replies.body: Also, if I did set the stop loss to 1-2% it wouldn’t work, I’d get eaten up by fees majority of the time. It’s so hard to actually predict a trade that just goes straight up, most my trades do EVENTUALLY go up or straight up but not before they dip a little which I think is normal. It’s almost impossible to predict a short/long if a coin will go straight up or down. It’s gotta go both ways before ending up in your preferred half.

replies.author: fomoz
replies.body: I just told you what's wrong. If you think you know better, then keep doing what you're doing.

replies.author: IllustratorSouth4671
replies.body: Is it possible to dm you?

comments.author: IllustratorSouth4671
comments.body:
An edge isn’t my problem I don’t think, I’m hitting 70-98% win rates, the actual problem is my losers run 4x the size of my winners which is a sizing/exit issue not a signal issue. 

Should I track MFE/MAE separately for winners vs losers? Trying to figure out if my losers ever go posited before reversing (timing/exit problem) or just go straight down (signal problem). Feel like that would tell me more then pricing a stop%

replies.author: thingygeoff
replies.body:
Like fomoz said, win rate is not a magic determiner of edge. If you are targeting 1x profit but have a 4x stop loss then mathematically in a completely random and neutral market simulation you would expect an average win rate of 80% with zero edge, just by placing entirely random trades.

I strongly recommend you flip what you’re trying to do, with a 2x or 3x target to a 1x stop loss. This is where you should be aiming. Perhaps initially try just 1:1, same target to stoploss, if you can make money like this then you are starting to find an edge, if you can’t, then you likely don’t have an edge. Your stoploss, target and position size should scale with price action and volatility, based on your strategy and its underlying theorem (more on this below)

Trading cliche: hold on to your winners, cut your losers - sounds straight forward, but actually hard to get right.

Risk management is essential. You should be dynamically sizing positions to keep your risk as a consistent percentage of your account (not a fixed amount per trade), the idea here being that your stoploss should go somewhere that means your strategy is no longer likely to win for that trade - the invalidation point. This means that your position size needs to be calculated dynamically from the invalidation point to the expected average entry price (not a fixed %).

By thinking in terms of invalidation it gives you a reason to put your stop there, which is important in finding an edge. It also means that if price has moved too far away from invalidation, then there might not be a trade, as conversely price may more be too close to the next target area. You should have a rational reason for what each part of your strategy does. Why the stop loss here, why enter here, why target here. Try aiming for a minimum RRR of 1, but ideally 2-4.

Sometimes it’s best to keep your strategy simple but make your filters advanced (when to avoid trades because the market conditions are not right). No trade is a very valid choice. Protecting your capital is probably more than half the battle.

The best traders (and often systems too) truly know when not to trade. You can make more money trading less, on a validated high quality edge, by increasing your position risk (dynamic sizing) or opening multiple positions (compounding) only for high probability setups, rather than trading every loose setup that comes along. But, you have to prove the edge first and recognise the difference between an A+ trade and a B or C trade. This is quite hard to do with a bot.

There is so much more to be aware of too: market structure, trending vs ranging, multi time-frame, compounding and dynamic sizing, knowing when to cut a trade early, volume and volume profile, individual market characteristics, wider market awareness, political and economic factors - don’t try to do everything, but make informed choices and strip down to focus on your niche.

Forget win ratio. Focus on timing and filtering to find the best setups and good risk management to protect capital.
